extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, and students of dramatic theory/poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive rules and evaluative criteria for composing and judging Greek tragedy: how to construct plot, character, thought, diction, music, spectacle, unity, magnitude, and the devices (reversal, recognition, pathos) that produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy as imitation of action (not men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation, not of men, but of an action and of life; dramatic action is primary, character is subsidiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose tragedy to imitate a complete action — the representation of action (plot/incidents) is the end of tragedy; avoid constructing a piece that is merely a sequence of character-expressive speeches. Example contrast: a play of well-finished speeches may fail to produce the tragic effect compared with a play having a constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (mythos) is the first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and the chief thing of all in tragedy; incidents and the plot are the end of a tragedy, and the end is the chief thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize construction of a coherent, causally integrated plot (beginning, middle, end). The poet should be the maker of plots rather than merely of verses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) holds second place
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is secondary to plot: character determines men’s qualities but it is by their actions that they are happy or the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should reveal moral purpose (what a man chooses or avoids) through their actions and choices; good portraiture/diction cannot substitute for a sound plot. Novices often achieve diction and portraiture before they can construct plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; in oratory it corresponds to political and rhetorical argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include speeches or moments that assert or prove what is or is not, or state general maxims appropriate to the situation. Thought contributes to conveying the reasoning and principles underlying action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) as expression in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to wording, formulation and verbal expression as vehicles of meaning; still, diction is subordinate to plot and thought for producing the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (melopoiia) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the embellishments, song holds the chief place among the pleasurable elements of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use musical/choral elements to embellish and heighten emotional effect, but keep them integrated with the dramatic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) is least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery and spectacle have emotional attraction but are the least artistic element and depend more on stagecraft than on the poet’s art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on scenic effects to achieve the essential tragic power; focus on plot and poetic construction since tragic power is felt apart from representation and actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must be an imitation of a whole action with magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates an action that is complete and whole and of a certain magnitude: a whole has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the work constitutes a complete action (not merely a fragment) and has appropriate magnitude so the unity and sense of the whole are perceptible to spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity, but after which something naturally is or comes to be; an end naturally follows some other thing and has nothing following it; a middle follows something and is followed by something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot points so they satisfy these causal relationships: beginnings should not presuppose previous events, ends should close causally, middles should connect logically between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper magnitude (length) of the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful whole must be of a certain magnitude — not so small as to be confused, nor so vast that the eye (memory) cannot take it all in; proper magnitude allows the sequence of events to admit a change from good fortune to bad or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep length such that the sequence of events is graspable by memory and allows the required transformations (e.g., from good to bad) to occur plausibly; theatrical contest/time constraints are not artistic rules but external limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (one action only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot is not unity of hero; the plot must imitate one action and be such that removing any part disjoints the whole: every part must be organically necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic accumulation of adventures that lack causal connection to the central action; ensure each episode is an organic part of the singular action the tragedy imitates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should represent what may happen (probability/necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet relates what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity, not merely what has happened; poetry expresses the universal (how persons of given character will act), while history records particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose actions that are credible under probability or necessity — plausible events that reveal general truths about character and action; historical fact is not required if the events conform to the probable/necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epeisodic plots (disconnected episodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots, where episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence, are the worst; they are produced by poor poets or by good poets yielding to external pressures (players/competition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make transitions and sequencing probabilistically or causally necessary; avoid stitching unrelated spectacles or incidents merely to please performers or extend performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy must excite pity and fear; surprise and causal connection heighten effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy imitates actions that are terrible and pitiful; the effect is best produced when events come by surprise and when they follow one another (causal/necessary sequence), increasing tragic wonder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineer plots so key sad/terrible events emerge unexpectedly yet as the necessary or probable outcome of preceding action (not as pure accident), producing stronger pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple actions are continuous changes without Reversal or Recognition; Complex actions include Reversal (peripeteia), Recognition (anagnorisis), or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer complex plots for a perfect tragedy because reversal and recognition (when arising from the internal structure of the plot) intensify pity and fear; simple plots lack these dramatic mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia) — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which a train of action produces the opposite of the effect intended (subject to probability/necessity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that arise from the plot’s internal logic and lead to unexpected but necessary outcomes (example: in Oedipus the messenger intending to cheer him produces the opposite). Reversal should be causal, not arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) — definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; best when coincident with reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct recognitions that reveal crucial knowledge (identity, deed, relation) and, ideally, coincide with reversal to maximize tragic emotion (example: Oedipus’ recognition). Recognitions may be between one party knowing the other or mutual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic incident (pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic incident (pathos) is a destructive or painful action — death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pathos as necessary to produce pity/fear, but ensure such incidents stem naturally from the plot’s causal structure rather than as mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exodos, choric song, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologos (part before Parodos), Episode (parts between complete choric songs), Exodos (part with no choric song after it), and choric parts: Parodos (first utterance of Chorus) and Stasimon (choric ode without anapaests/trochees); Commos is a lament of Chorus and actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these structural divisions appropriately; know functions of each section (e.g., Parodos opens chorus, Stasimon is stationary chorus ode, Commos is joint lament) and integrate them into the dramatic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition should be complex and imitate fearful and pitiable actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged on the complex plan and should imitate actions which excite pity and fear — this is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that show virtuous men brought to misfortune (which arouse neither pity nor fear), or villains made prosperous (which arouse no pity/fear); instead choose a protagonist of stature who falls through an error or frailty (hamartia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tragic protagonist (middle character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be neither eminently good and just nor utterly bad; his misfortune should stem from some error or frailty (not from vice), and he should be of high standing brought from prosperity to adversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a hero whose fall through error provokes both pity (unmerited suffering) and fear (a man like ourselves suffering), rather than a wholly virtuous or wholly villainous figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic necessity of incidents (internal causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals, recognitions, and episodes must arise from the internal structure of the plot so that subsequent events follow by necessity or probability from preceding ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the plot so surprises and shifts appear as necessary or probable consequences of earlier acts and dispositions rather than as accidents or contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length must be memorable and suitable to the action’s transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must have a length which can be easily embraced by memory; the proper magnitude permits the sequence of events (by probability/necessity) to admit a change from good fortune to bad or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes of size: not so small that the view is confused, not so large that unity is lost. Choose a scale that supports the central transformation and unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity is not unity of the hero nor inclusion of all incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot does not consist in centring on all incidents of a hero’s life; many events in one man’s life cannot be reduced to one action, so the poet should select incidents that centre on one action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to include all adventures or biographical incidents of a hero; instead centre the work on a single coherent action (as Homer does in the Odyssey and Iliad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of familiar vs. invented material
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to stick to received legends; both familiar and fictitious names/incidents may give pleasure, provided they are possible and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feel free to invent plots or names if they conform to probability/necessity and serve the unity and emotional effect of the tragedy; reliance on traditional myths is not obligatory.
